utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Again only two Judges are present. Judge Mindua is still absent today and tomorrow. Pursuant to Rule 15 bis, we are sitting with two Judges only. If there are no procedural matters, the witness should be brought in. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Judge Nyambe, and everyone. I've got a bit of a flu/cold bug, but I hopefully will get through it no problem. And this witness, I would request he receive a caution, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to this court. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Salapura. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. On the request of the Prosecution, I have to caution you, and I would like to read out the specific Rule. This is Rule 90(e) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and I quote: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Mr. Salapura, did you understand what I was reading to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey is now putting questions to you in his examination-in-chief. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And good afternoon, sir. Could you tell us your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us your position in the VRS when you left.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The Chief of the Intelligence Service of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you leave the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Officially in 1997. Before that already in the second half of the -- of 1996 I was sent on vacation, and I was placed at disposal for six months. I left the Main Staff officially in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And before we get into the events of July 1995, let me ask you a couple of things. First of all, did you testify as a Defence witness for the -- Colonel Blagojevic in the Blagojevic/Jokic case that was held here at the ICTY a few years back?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to listen to your testimony from that trial?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you stand by your -- your testimony of that trial?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after that trial, were you interviewed by an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review the transcript of -- of that interview?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you stand by what was recorded in that interview and what you said in that interview?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your experience testifying here and being interviewed by the OTP, did you find any -- anything inappropriate or troublesome about how you were dealt with by anyone or any institution?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you give us a -- just a brief background. Let's start with the -- where you were born and the year of your birth.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was born on the 20th of August, 1948, in the village of Bjelaj in Bosanski Petrovac municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you are a professional military officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us a brief outline of your -- when you graduated from the important military schools and -- and your main jobs as you progressed throughout your career.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: From the very beginning, I graduated from the land army military academy in 1971. I -- I was in infantry. I started working at the Zagreb garrison as a platoon commander. After a year, I was reassigned to start working in Virovitica where I was a company commander for two years, and after that I served in Koprivnica again for two years. From Koprivnica, I was moved to Karlovac. I was a member of the security services there for seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us your rank there at Karlovac so we -- and tell us your rank so we can see that progression?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: In Karlovac my rank was captain and captain first class, and then I became major. I was promoted. And then I was reassigned to work in Zagreb. I believe that that was in 1983. I was assigned to work at the command of the 5th Army. I was a member of the intelligence department. I was an analyst. From there, from Zagreb, I went to Bihac as a brigade commander, as a lieutenant-colonel. My promotion to the rank of major was early. I was a brigade commander until 1988. In 1988, I was sent to the former Soviet Union where I graduated from the Command Staff Academy Voroshilov. I returned in 1990. I returned to Zagreb, and that's where I was when the war started. I didn't say that even before that I graduated from the Command Staff Academy of the Army of Yugoslavia as it was then known. It was in Belgrade. That was in 1981. Actually, I was in school from 1981 to 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What subjects were you taught when you were at the Soviet Union, just roughly. I'm not going to get into a lot about the Soviet Union, but I do want to ask you what you were learning over there.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That was a General Staff academy, and there were a lot of subjects taught there, all at the strategical level of education just like in any other military in the world. Those were mostly military subject, and the main focus was strategy and operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about intelligence work? Did you learn methods and processes of military intelligence work at the Soviet Union?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. No. That was only part of the operations planning. Nothing special was taught. That was one of the things that were thought to provide support during operations. I was educated for a command duty over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you first meet General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I believe that that was in 1967 or perhaps 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you -- did you become friends with him at some point in your military career?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, we graduated from the academy together, and then he was sent to Macedonia, I believe, and then we didn't see each other before the beginning of the last war. I mean, not before 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And 1991, can you just tell us briefly what your assignments were there, just very briefly. I want to get us to the spring of 1992 pretty quickly.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say what my assignments were? I don't know where -- what assignments do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, well, for example, when the fighting began in Vukovar, you were in the JNA, I take it. Where were you assigned, anywhere near the fighting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was not in Vukovar. I was not in that area. I was a member of the 5th Military District in Zagreb. I was a member of the command of that military district in Zagreb. When the war started, I was the chief of the education department, the department for the combat education of the troops and the officers, and after that I also took over the intelligence department, because the Croatian officers had already started leaving the JNA because the conflict had started in Croatia. The relationships were rather tense. And I stayed there until the end as an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you first have contact with General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I believe that that was sometime in late 1991 or perhaps early 1992. There was a training course in Knin for intelligence officers. I attended the course as one of the lecturers, and that's where I encountered Tolimir. That was our first encounter after we had been at the academy together. And that was a very brief meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was General Tolimir a student or a lecturer or something else at that point?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He was serving in Knin at the time. He was the chief of security in the Knin Corps. I believe that he was also in charge of a topic, or perhaps one of his subordinates. I can't tell you exactly. The training course took several days .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I ask for a moment. Do you have a problem with the chair? Is it perhaps not in the right position? Do you have a problem with that or is everything fine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm fine. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the Knin Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know what position Mr. Beara had at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know him. I had not even heard of him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you become a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: From the moment it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember what month that was? April, May 1992, or just roughly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what assignment did you get?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Up to then I was the chief of the intelligence department of the 5th Army District. It was renamed as the 2nd Military District, and the seat of that military district was in Sarajevo. I was the chief of the same department in the 2nd Military District when the VRS was established, and then I automatically became the chief of the intelligence department in the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you hold that position, the chief of the intelligence department of the VRS, throughout the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: There was a reorganisation later. At the beginning, the VRS was established according to the military district establishment of the former JNA. The department was later transformed into an administration, which is why I remained serving as the chief of the intelligence administration of the Main Staff. However, having said that, my assignments were practically the same. They didn't change. They were identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did it change from what you briefly described as the JNA formation to an administration under the VRS? Just roughly again.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly when that happened. I believe that that was sometime in the second half of 1992, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, because we are interested in the structure as it was in 1995. So -- but from the second half of 1992, roughly to the end of 1995, was there any significant changes in the structure, in the administrative structure, of the Main Staff as you knew it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were some changes within the Main Staff, but only on paper. However when it comes to the numerical strength and the number of staff, there weren't any major changes. We just didn't have enough people according to the establishment. I believe that my administration only had 15 per cent of the men envisaged by the establishment. Later on, a sector for intelligence was set up, and that co-ordinated the work of both administrations. This was done in order to rationalise staff and know-how. My administration was particularly short dealt because we didn't have enough people. The security administration had more men. So, under the umbrella of the sector, people from the security services were also charged with gathering intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You stated that a sector for intelligence was set up and that it co-ordinated the work of both administrations, and then you mentioned security. So did you mean that a sector of intelligence and security was set up to handle both intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as the chief of intelligence, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: What period do you have in mind? In 1992, when it was set up, it was the Chief of Staff for a brief period of time when we had departments. Once the administration was set up, then it was the administration for security and intelligence with the two departments, and the chief of that administration was General Tolimir, who was a colonel at the time. Later on when the sector was set up, the chief of that sector was General Tolimir, and he was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So if General Tolimir was the chief of intelligence and security for the sector, did he have another job at the same time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. He was the chief of the sector and also the assistant commander for the same area. I believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to us if there's any difference between -- any practical difference between the chief of the sector for intelligence and security and an assistant commander for intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, no. No. There is no difference. That person performs the same duties. The commander had assistants for logistics, for intelligence and security, for personnel and several others. I don't even know who they were. There was also an assistant for morale and propaganda and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So you've mentioned the security. I believe you called it an administration. Was there the -- a chief of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that throughout most of the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Colonel -- well, throughout the war it was Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his first name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I think his name is Ljubisa. We called him Ljubo. I believe his full name is Ljubisa Beara, but we all called him Ljubo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you briefly name for us the people that worked under you in the intelligence administration in 1995. We're especially concerned about July 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I think so. It was Lieutenant-Colonel Jovica Karanovic; Radoslav Jankovic, also lieutenant-colonel; then Slobodan Mamlic, I believe he was a major or also lieutenant-colonel, I'm not sure about that; Warrant Officer Boro, or rather, full name Borislav Isakovic. And sometime in June, Milovan Stankovic joined the administration. He was reassigned to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just tell us --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just tell us the title of Lieutenant-Colonel Karanovic's position? What was he doing? Just the title. I don't want to, at this point, go into the description.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He was chief of section for analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about Radoslav Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Radoslav Jankovic was a desk officer in the same section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Lieutenant-Colonel Mamlic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He was chief of section for electronic reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And any other significant officers in your -- in your administration?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I've mentioned already at that time we were joined by Milovan Stankovic. I didn't even get to see him there. And he became chief of section for intelligence work with troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And before we go into more specifics about the -- the Main Staff, can you describe generally -- and we've heard some of this before, so I just want you to ask [sic] just generally. We know, the Judges know, that the VRS is divided roughly into several corps. Each of those corps have brigades, and that each of those brigades have battalions, and in each -- each of those levels there are intelligence officers. So could you, first of all, tell us out in the field, the brigades and the corps, practically, what is the job of the intelligence officer, just simply?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, intelligence officers dealt exclusively with collecting intelligence on the enemy, on the lay of the land, as we called it, on the enemy's side, enemy facilities, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the Trial Chamber has also learned that in a Light Infantry Brigade like the Bratunac Brigade, the intelligence officer is also the officer for security. Basically he is an intelligence and security officer, and that as we go up into a larger brigade like the Zvornik Brigade, it's divided, where there is an intelligence officer and a security officer, and it's the same in the corps, it's divided in the corps. But then when we get back to the Main Staff, we see again that General Tolimir is intelligence and security. So can you tell us what is this connection between intelligence and security? So if you could roughly tell us, what is it that security officers do, and what is this connection that we're seeing represented in the structures? How does it play out practically?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, a security officer deals with security and counter-intelligence, that is to say, internal problems within units, the units of the army Republika Srpska, and in the areas of responsibility or of operation of these units. That involves certain tasks that fall within the competence of military courts and military prosecutors' offices, and he also professionally manages military police and reconnaissance units, for example. In light brigades of smaller strength, this title is dual, and it is vested in the assistant Chief of Staff, but that is to say one person would pursue both these lines of work, whereas intelligence officers deal exclusively with collecting intelligence on the enemy, on the other side of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do security officers also seek information and have confidential informants?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, they seek information on the enemy as well if they are able to get any, and they always take the opportunity if it arises. As for confidential informants, as far as their work is concerned within the units of the Army of Republika Srpska, they did have some.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as an intelligence --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Whether they had sources in enemy units, I wouldn't know. That was their secret. Just as they are unaware of our sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would the ground intelligence, the people on your side of the work, would they -- would you have intelligence sources on the enemy's strategies and operations, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: You mean on the enemy's side. In their units on the enemy territory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And going back to my original question, what is the relationship between security and intelligence? Why does it make sense, for example, for the Main Staff to have General Tolimir over both administrations, and why does it make sense in a light brigade to have someone who handles both those administrations? What do these things have in common that they're joined like that sometimes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Let's start with the light infantry brigade. It's a smaller brigade with lower strength, and it was probably evaluated long before the war that one person would be capable of dealing with both functions. On brigade level, the intelligence component is not so prominent. It boils down to scouting work, reconnaissance, et cetera. On the Main Staff level things, get very different. It is only there that intelligence work involves operations. Since these operations are handled by the security service, the security service in their work gets to receive a lot of information that is interesting to the intelligence administration, and they also get information on people who are not interesting to them, but they are interesting to the intelligence administration. Also, sometimes people from the intelligence administration who deal with operational work also get such information. However, earlier this information was not collated between them. It was archived, filed. And that's why a person was put ultimately at the top, to be able to decide who will get what information, what will be referred to whom, in order to avoid duplication and -- and the crossing of competencies. Also, the intelligence administration had a dearth of staff, and with just one person at the top at sector level were we able to more fully staff the security service in such a way that they would be better engaged in intelligence work and pass on the information to the intelligence administration. It was an arrangement that was dictated by necessity in our circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned that the security got involved in operations. Can you -- what was their fundamental responsibility, security's responsibility, in operations as you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I didn't mention operations. If you mean intelligence activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said that it is only there that intelligence work involves operations, and you said, "Since these operations are handled by the security service, the security service in their work gets to receive a lot of information." So I was asking you how is security work related to a military operation. Just a very brief highlight, if you could, based on your experience. It seems to me you were distinguishing intelligence involved in operations and security.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, all this is in the service of operations, if you call it operations, both components, but what I was trying to say is that intelligence organs in their work got by a lot of intelligence that was simply not useful, not interesting to them. And they just rejected it, if I can put it that way. And they did not look into ways of collating it, and we in the intelligence organs were very poorly staffed and very poorly equipped, and we needed all the information available on the enemy, and that's why we needed the other sector to pass the information on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let me interrupt you. You said they got a lot of information that was not useful to them. Were you referring to the security branch?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I meant the security branch. Yes, yes. They had information about the enemy, and that was not their field of work. What they dealt with was the internal work within the units, within the Army of Republika Srpska, and they were involved in counter-intelligence. And, of course, they got also external information about the enemy, their strength, their intentions, et cetera, and they -- they were able to -- to pass it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us practically, let's use the year of 1995, did you share information with Beara and Beara's administration, the security administration at the level of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: We forwarded our information to all the organs of the Main Staff including the security administration. All the intelligence was passed on. And our security information got our brief on the enemy every day about the enemy's intentions on the entire territory of Republika Srpska. That's what the administration did, and the corps worked at their own level. From the security administration we received only information that was interesting and relevant to us. We did not receive security-related information regarding internal problems, technical stuff, et cetera. We only received information from them if they happened to have any about the disposition of the enemy, the strength, their intentions, possible axis of action, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just practically let me see if I can give you an example of an internal problem, an internal security problem. Would such a problem be, for example, a brigade commander that was stealing? Would that be a security, an internal problem that you really probably wouldn't be interested in?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That was of absolutely no interest to the intelligence service. That is strictly a security problem. They deal with it, whether he stole money or ammunition or, for instance, case of desertion or whatever they did. That's their problem. There's a lot of that kind. Or perhaps a person was working for the enemy intelligence service, passing on information. That's the kind of thing they dealt with. Or perhaps somebody was getting ready to escape, desert, create a problem in the army, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe briefly your job. What did you do basically, but simply and how did you relate to the subordinate units, the corps and the brigade? We -- the Judges have heard a lot about this professional line. Can you just give us a brief description of your job and how you relate it to the corps and down to the brigade, if you did.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: We only worked on collecting intelligence on the enemy, I repeat. But we were also interested in intelligence on the activities of the international community, because we were looking for a way to end the war. Our service also dealt with contacts and activities further afield with similar institutions and organisations in other neighbouring countries, countries in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And before I ask you --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: And further afield, of course. That was the professional organ that proposed how to use personnel, guided, equipped, prepared, and described information obtained by scouting and reconnaissance units, only for the purpose of executing scouting and reconnaissance -- sabotage and reconnaissance tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll get into that a little bit more, but can you tell us at the Main Staff what kind of reports you made, regular reports, that is, and who did you send them to, and what kind of reports did you receive from others on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, we regularly received information from subordinate units, from the corps, and then our analysis section analysed those reports from the corps and also from the intelligence centres, the institution that dealt with operational intelligence work that was part of the intelligence administration. We received reports from them daily. The analysis section compiled it all and provided a daily summary. That summary was provided to subordinate units, to the chief of sector, General Tolimir, and he would then write in the top corner who that needed to be passed on, Chief of Staff, corps commander, assistant for moral guidance or something. I can't really enumerate all the copies. And then the chief of sector would also add his own addressees to whom that was to be copied depending on the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And these -- these daily intel reports to General Tolimir, whose name would they go out under?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: You mean -- well, you would see sector for intelligence work, intelligence administration in the heading. That was an intelligence report process. If I was at the command post, I would sign it. If in my absence, Jovica Karanovic would sign it, and if even he wasn't there, then Mamlic would sign it, and he would then forward that information to General Tolimir. There were also special reports as a result of some special interviews or extraordinary work or my own activities. Then General Tolimir would look at it and indicate at the top to whom that was to be copied and what kind of action needed to be taken. These were no regular reports or briefs, they were, as we call it, interim reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General Tolimir, can you describe his job? As the chief of intel and security or assistant commander for intel and security, which you tell us is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He co-ordinated the work of both institutions, and he guided the work of my service. I don't know what his relationship was with the security service, because he never had a joint meeting with me and Beara, for instance. He had a separate meeting with me and a separate meeting with Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "guided"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Directed. He would decide on a thrust of activity and its focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he have the right to command over you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: How do you mean could he command me? He was my superior, yes, and he had the right to give me orders about anything that needed to be done by the intelligence administration and intelligence organs. I was directly subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he bear responsibility for your actions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, of course, before his commander. If we did something wrong, if we did something badly, although I wasn't present, but he would probably have been told off and rebuked by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But militarily, can you describe that responsibility? What is it that he as your superior has responsibility for? I mean, he gets credit for the good things that you do as well as the bad, but can you describe what that responsibility is in the military --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. His responsibility was for the work of the administration, the scope of information, the -- the quality of information gathered by my service, if we are talking about my case, because the commander sees all these reports. He receives them daily, just as he receives reports from other organs, and he could summon Tolimir any time and say, "I'm not pleased with this. Look into it, Tolimir. Deal with this problem. Pay more attention to this or that," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: And he also -- and he knows best about that. He also had other obligations and duties within the Staff Command, there were negotiations with UNPROFOR, with the Bosniak side, with the Croatian side. As an assistant commander, he participated in those activities. That was part of his duties as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said a while back that sometimes intelligence people make proposals to their superior. Can you -- did you make proposals for specific actions to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he sometimes take those proposals and issue you orders in furtherance of them or issue orders to others that would be responsible for carrying them out if it wasn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Absolutely. We had a fair and correct relationship, open relationship, and, yes, whenever he would have any objection, he would immediately tell me about it, give his suggestions how to improve things. I may have had some proposals that had to do with the working of the command or the relationships there. He accepted those or not and then informed the commander about it or not. That's a normal way of functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you also explain --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I apologise. On occasions, he would ask me for a proposal or suggestion and sometimes he wouldn't ask me for anything of the kind. Sometimes he would want to compare his views with mine. He would ask me what your views are on this topic or that topic and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if you, in your position, offered a proposal to General Tolimir and he agreed with it and issued you an order to carry it out, let's say for the use of the 10th Sabotage Detachment to go do reconnaissance work somewhere in the Krajina, would you have any responsibility to follow up on that operation to determine how that operation went, or is it that once the orders are issued it's hands off?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Tolimir could not order something like that. He could have made a proposal to the commander who would then issue an order and then Tolimir would tell me about such an order. You mentioned the 10th Sabotage and Reconnaissance Detachment. It was an independent unit of the Main Staff that was directly subordinated to the commander of the Main Staff. The intelligence administration was an organ that was in charge of providing support in equipment, weapons, in training for both officers and soldiers to give proposals for operations, both attack operations and defence operations, to issue tasks or proposals about the tasks for such a unit. For instance, go and reconnaissance such a feature or explain some specific task. That's something that is then proposed to the commander, and then the commander issues his orders to the unit. It is also possible and it would happen often that some of the intelligence officers at the lower levels would be tasked with that, but that would be an intelligence officer who was in charge of preparations for an assignment. For instance, if a group would be sent behind the enemy lines for reconnaissance or sabotage activities, now, that would be specifically under the responsibilities of the detachment commander, and he would then report after completing his mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's take the example, the first one you mentioned where based on your proposal General Tolimir takes a proposal to use the 10th Sabotage Detachment to go to the Krajina to do surveillance and General Mladic agrees and issues the order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, no, no. General Tolimir cannot reach such a decision. He can propose and only propose something like that to General Mladic. General Mladic is the only person who can make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's what I was saying so just hear me out. General Tolimir takes your proposal to General Mladic and we understand then General Mladic agrees with General Tolimir's proposal, which originated from you, and issues the order for the 10th Sabotage to go. What are General Tolimir's responsibilities in monitoring this operation or anything else or does he have none?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He has this responsibility upon hearing my proposal. After having thought about it he says, yes, this is okay or no, this will not do. He can say, No, I cannot make such a proposal to the commander because the consequences of it would be such and such or we do not have sufficient guarantees that this unit would complete the mission and return, that people would not die, all of them in the unit would not die, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me take you to something you said in the last trial at page 10544, and let me know if you agree with this. The question was: "Now, also in going back to the intel model, once the commander makes a decision on how to use, in your situation, the recon platoon, would the intel officer be responsible for seeing to it that the commander's orders were carried out?" And you answered: "Yes." And you said: "He would be the one who would monitor the entire implementation and get involved in the preparing a specific unit for a specific task. He monitors the entire course of implementation, and he is responsible for the orders to be carried out pursuant to the commander's order. He has been trained for that, and he is the most qualified person or should be." That's what I meant to be asking you. Do you stand by that -- that answer you gave?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Peace to this house and hello, Mr. Salapura. I hope he will enjoy his stay here. I hope he will return home safely, and let this day go according to God's will and not mine. Now, Mr. McCloskey named page P10444 of a trial, but he didn't specific which trial so that we can identify it, so that we don't have to search for it for a long time, because the witness will be here tomorrow again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you said the last trial. Which one was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's been only one trial that the witness has testified in and that's Blagojevic, and it's only in English, of course, so it doesn't really help. That's why I just read it slowly, and I usually read things correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not a problem. We just wanted to know which trial. You said it, Blagojevic. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Colonel, do the responsibilities that you had set out here, to monitor, et cetera, would that apply to General Tolimir? He proposed the use of a particular unit and that order had been carried out by General Mladic? Would he have to follow up on that as you've described here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, and it gets transferred to me. Normally if the operation fails, General Mladic would criticise him, maybe take some measures, even, but the responsibility gets transferred more to the intelligence administration in this issue, because it's the intelligence administration that is monitoring all the preparations for the operation up until the moment of sending the units to carry out the mission. From that moment it's the commander of the detachment who's responsible. That's a specific point. That would be a secret. Even I didn't know, for instance, when that unit would cross over into the enemy territory. Not even General Tolimir would know about it. Not even General Mladic would know about that. We are talking, of course, of ideal conditions when I myself am present and General Tolimir is present, and so on, but very often, especially during 1995, I was, for instance, absent for 90 per cent of the time. He was also very often absent. So it would have been somebody else who would be acting in our absence, but what I mean is the intelligence organ or the security organ. Very often I would be the one who would go to the commander with a proposal instead of him, because, for instance, he was not -- I mean, Mr. Tolimir was not familiar with the issue at hand because he had been absent for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, we'll get to the facts of this case and where people were soon enough. It's a very simple question. The Judges have heard an answer to this question several times, and let me try it again. When an assistant commander makes a proposal to General Mladic and General Mladic takes that proposal and issues an order, does that assistant commander bear responsibility to monitor the carrying out of that order and implementation of that order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, he does bear responsibility of some sort, maybe moral, maybe even disciplinary before the commander of the Main Staff, but he cannot -- General Tolimir cannot go and monitor how ten soldiers are training and preparing in the region of Banja Luka, for instance, because such preparations can last for 10 to 15 days. He cannot be there personally and watch them all the time. And last and at least, this is about the proposal part. Neither I could have gone there and spent the time. We would assign someone from the corps, a clerk, a duty officer, who would go and report to me about the potential problem, and then if I cannot take care of the problem, then I inform General Tolimir about it, because maybe his influence and authority can make the problem go away. If there is a way for me to handle it, then I don't bother him with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting responsibility is to the lower individual as opposed to the higher individual? You seem to suggest that the commander of the 10th Sabotage would bear more responsibility for the action rather than his superior, General Mladic, or the person that recommended the use of the 10th Sabotage. And I'm talking about a recon mission, sir. We're not at Branjevo farm yet. We will get there.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes, I understand, but this is not at all related to the professional line, the events at the Branjevo farm. This was an entirely different thing. No, I'm not saying that he does not have responsibility. The commander of the detachment, who was a captain or a lieutenant, he has the same responsibility as the commander of a regiment or a brigade. It's an independent unit. And I'm not saying that I don't have a responsibility there or that General Tolimir does not have at least partial responsibility, but if we would monitor every detail and every group, I don't know, what would we achieve? The one who has made the proposal, let's say it was the detachment commander or the commander of the Drina Corps there, it's their intelligence officer who explains in detail in his report why and how if we're talking about the reconnaissance mission. And then you have a layer of filter which goes through detachment commander, myself. I need to know whether there is any guarantee that mission would be successful, that the losses won't be too big. And after I've made an assessment, if I'm convinced that there is actually a chance of this mission succeeding, then -- then I go to General Tolimir with my proposal, or if he's absent to the commander, and then I am responsible to the commander for any failure of such a mission. We would be -- I would be the one in this case who would have to face the commander and face his criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Exactly. And because of that would you monitor the carrying out of that operation? Would you want regular reports on that operation to see how it went?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I cannot directly monitor it. These are very small groups. I do not monitor them directly. There is someone in charge of monitoring them, and the detachment commander will report to me if there are any problems. Most probably also some of the intelligence officers from lower levels will be monitoring the preparations and inform me about those and inform me about any problems encountered, because maybe my help is required. And once the preparations are completed, I'm informed about that, and I'm informed that the units can go out and carry out its mission. Now, the commander of the unit is the only person who can decide about the timing of the mission. Now, in 15 minutes, tonight, next morning. That's something I know nothing about. That's a secret that only the commander of the unit knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can a corps intel officer command one of these 10th Sabotage operations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. Providing the unit was resubordinated to him. Such a unit can be resubordinated to the corps command for a certain mission. The commander of the Main Staff can say, okay, this unit will be resubordinated to the Drina Corps or some other corps. We have had situations when a group would be resubordinated to the 1st Krajina Corps for a specific mission, or the Drina Corps. The commander may issue such an order without asking either myself or Tolimir. We don't even know anything about that. Commander issued an order that this unit should carry out such and such a mission upon the request of a commander of some other corps. That's part of the prerogatives of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you said you wouldn't personally monitor, and I think we understand that from Crna Rijeka or even a forward command post. You're not going on the recon mission, but you do have people reporting up the professional chain from the brigades and the corps intel people providing you daily reports, including special reports. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- we'll begin to get into some more of the practical workings of these issues which we've already gotten into a bit, so let's get to 1995, and were you carrying out your work, as you've described, normally throughout most of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Not only throughout 1995, throughout the entire period. Between 1992 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you familiar that there were several directives that came out either in the name of General Mladic or President Karadzic throughout the war? I believe there was nine of them.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know how many, how many there were. I -- I may have participated in planning of maybe two or three of them, and I know that one or two of them were not even implemented, but I did not participate in drafting the directives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you have testified before that for health reasons you were aware from the Main Staff for a period of time. Can you tell us when that was --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That was from late June. General Tolimir is here. Am I allowed to ask him if he could help me identify the precise dates --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: -- because it would be -- fine, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's not possible. Mr. McCloskey is putting questions to you, and Mr. Tolimir is not testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. It's fine, it's fine, it's fine. That was after the 20th of June, but I cannot be more precise. Between the 20th and 25th of June. I went to General Tolimir. I had some serious health problems. It was something that was going on for a while already at the time. I was not away either on vacation or in any other way since 1990, except for two days when I was absent. Then I had problems with intestines, mucous tissue, and all sorts of intestinal problems, and I also had chronic problems with my spine. It's still persistent. And I was exhausted, in a very difficult condition mentally. I asked General Tolimir in writing to be relieved of duty. I just could not handle it any more. I was busy all the time, 24 hours a day. And he managed to persuade me to change my mind, which I did. I went to our doctor, and I was recommended to stay away for a month on sick leave, but I could not stay away for a whole month. He -- General Tolimir told me, "You know, go away for treatment to Banja Luka. Stay away for a month, and I will co-ordinate all the activities here in the eastern part, and you try and follow what is going on in the western part. You also monitor what's going on with Croatian preparations," because we already did have some intelligence about Croatian Army intentions there. So this was -- I was in charge of the 1st and the 2nd Corps. And after this discussion with General Tolimir, I went to Banja Luka. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I want to be clear. You mentioned June 20th to the 25th. Was that the time period you were off, or were you -- did you leave at that -- some point between those five days?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It's between the 20th and 25th that I left for a period of a -- of one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what date did you come back to work?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Back to work? Well, I was in Banja Luka. I would spend a lot of time at the doctor's, and I was a lot of time at home, but occasionally they would bring some materials to me either from the centre in Banja Luka or maybe on occasion I would go directly there if there was something that only I could resolve. And I returned -- you mean, when was it that I returned to Han Pijesak? On the 12th -- or, rather, on the 11th. On the 11th, I was informed by the centre in Banja Luka that I'm expected in Belgrade on the 12th for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get -- we'll get into that, but were you at all aware of the situation in the Srebrenica and the Zepa enclaves as it was building up in the spring of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was aware. We were receiving information from the Drina Corps. The Drina Corps was monitoring the situation in the enclaves, both in Srebrenica and Zepa. We were also interested in the situation there, because Zepa is, yeah, several kilometres distance away from the Main Staff. There were many attacks launched from these enclaves, incursions, sabotage actions. There were killings of shepherds. There was rustling of cattle. We intervened with UNPROFOR, asking them to put a stop to it, but it did not bear any results.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we have heard that in February, March -- and in March there was a directive that was issued by President Karadzic that was drafted and assembled by the operations branch, General Miletic of the Main Staff, and that each of the organs, including your organ, played a role in assembling that, and that was Directive 7. Were you -- did you play a role in direct -- in assembling information for Directive 7, which came out in early March 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was not aware of the directive. I was not a participant in its drafting. I didn't even know that it was being prepared. I claim with full responsibility that people who were members of my organ didn't know either. As far as I know, I learned of that directive only in 1997. That's when I learned that it had been done. Lazic, an operative in the Drina Corps, told me that, and he was one of those who had participated in its drafting. I suppose that that was done by the commanders in a circle consisting of his assistants. I believe that a lot of intelligence information went into the directive, and they could have been obtained from the Drina Corps. And in the ops room there was a detailed map, an intelligence map which was updated every day by intelligence officers. And if you consulted the computer, you could have the updated information on Zepa and Srebrenica in five minutes, and that could have been provided either to Tolimir or Miletic. That was our obligation. We as intelligence officers were obliged to do that without even knowing what the purpose of that exercise was. I heard about that directive from you when I was interviewed by the OTP. I didn't know about it before that, and I was not involved in the preparation of that directive. I believe that you can find that in some of General Mladic's interviews. He said that all the operations that had been planned at that level were secret and that all the plans were made by the inner circle of commanders. That was the methodology of work that was used at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last question. Colonel, you were cross-examined by me on June 8th, 2004, and are you saying here today that that is the first time, June 8th, 2004, that you learned about Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Absolutely. I can swear on my own life. Not only that, the others as well. I never participated in any such thing. There was no reason for me to participate. First of all, I don't know who made plans. The Drina Corps carried out assignments, but I don't know what the role of the Main Staff was in all that. The Drina Corps was in charge of all the operations, not any other corps. And there are a lot of those that I was not aware of, not only that one. There were a lot of directives that I was not aware of. And there was no need for me to be aware of them. The commander could make decisions and draft them with the Chief of Staff, the chief of sectors, his inner circle of trusted men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Mr. President. In fact, I'm sorry, it's beyond break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. One clarification, please. Sir, you mentioned a moment ago a meeting in Belgrade on the 12th. Which month are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] June. Or, rather, July. I apologise. It was July. July. July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said on the 11th you were informed by the centre in Banja Luka that you were expected in Belgrade on the 12th for a meeting. These two dates have been in July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Both days in July, on the 11th and on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have our first break now, and we will resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm sorry to go backwards a little bit, but something you mentioned about the intelligence centres. Can you tell us what these intelligence centres was? In fact, I seem to remember something about the 410th Intelligence Centre. What was that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: There was just one, just one intelligence centre. That was the intelligence centre of the intelligence administration of the Main Staff. Those people were mainly agents who did operative work. There was just one such centre, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the name of it in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The 410th Intelligence Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the top man at the centre? Who was the commander of it or the chief of it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Cedo Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who else -- who worked under him or with him there in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Do you want me to give you the names of all the operatives? For example, Dusko Kenjalo. Slavuljica, Zare. Now you've caught me. The brain's gone. I really don't know. I don't think that it really matters. They were involved in operative work. They were agents who collected intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you -- do you know a person named Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. I know him, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's his -- what's his first name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Dragomir Pecanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his position in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He was the chief of General Mladic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was that job?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I really can't tell you exactly what he did. He was the chief of his office. He prepared certain materials for the commander. He prepared meetings for him, negotiations. There was his security, and I suppose he liaised with the security. There was another secretary. I really don't know what his authorities were. I suppose that he also looked after the commander's security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to where we left off, and that was the Directive 7, and I think we remember your answer to that. And if we could go to P1214. That will be up on the screen, and you should see the Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the English could we go to the next page, because that's just the cover, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see that this is dated 8 March of 1995 from the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska, and I'll tell you it's -- it's signed at the end by Radovan Karadzic, and it's drafted by General Miletic and typed by Staff Sergeant Spasoje Zeljkovic. Do you know Sergeant Zeljkovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Spasoje Zeljkovic, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. There's a -- a page in English displayed at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I want to start with the "Muslim-Croat Coalition Forces," paragraph 2. So we need to go to the next page in the B/C/S too, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, I don't want to spend a lot of time with a lot of this, but you'll agree with me that this is intel information on the -- on the Federation forces, won't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. This is an overview of the current situation in the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's -- let's go to the next page in English, paragraph 2.1.1 entitled "Muslim Armed Forces." Page 5. And, again, I don't want to get into the detail of it, but we can see here under "Muslim Armed Forces," "Probable objective and plans of the Muslim forces." That's all intelligence information; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we continue going through this we get to the next page in the English, a section titled "Armed forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna," and it talks about their objectives. Then we go on to the next page, and it's page upon page upon page, until page 7 in the English.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And page 11 in the B/C/S, which is all intel information. Who drafted this for General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know who drafted this. I'm sure that the intel was taken from an analyst. It could be done at Miletic's request, the sector's request, or General Tolimir could take the intel from the sector and word the information as he wanted. I certainly did not participate -- participate in this. I didn't even know that that was drafted. Things were updated on a daily basis, and you could obtain information from the computer within the matter of five to ten minutes, just like you do it now here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's why I ask you. I don't draft all of my motions. The Judges don't draft all of their decisions. We have people that do this, just like where you were.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you suggesting that General Tolimir did the drafting or that General Miletic did the drafting? Sir, you were the chief of intelligence. Who drafted this so that General Miletic could put it in and it could be reviewed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: One of the analysts could have provided the intel. I don't know who was there in March. It could have been Karanovic or Jankovic. They could have down -- downloaded the intel from the computer and give it to Miletic. General Tolimir could have requested the intel, and the group who participated in the drafting of the directive. I don't even know who participated. I know that Miletic did. It should not have been a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were alive and well and at work at Crna Rijeka at the time and you can't even tell us who drafted this, and you knew nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't think that I was in Crna Rijeka at the time. Let me tell you, the methodology of work was such that when the directives were drafted it was done by the commander and his inner circle. Nobody else knew about that. That was the style of work that the commander of the Main Staff had adopted. So the rest of us did not know what was going on, and I'm sure that many of the chiefs of different combat arms didn't know what was going on. There was a group of people involved in the drafting, and I don't know who those people were. I'm only sure that I was not one of them. Second of all, I was in Crna Rijeka, but I told you already that I spent very little time there. I was mostly absent. I was in the field, and I believe that you have intelligence privy to you and that you will see that my signature is missing from a lot of it. I really can't remember where I was on the day that that was drafted, but I'm sure I did not participate in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for one question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one more thing. I didn't know -- go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said, "I don't even know who participated." And then the next sentence, "I know General Miletic did." How do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that General Miletic could do this and that and the other. He was an operative, a person who united the whole thing. General Miletic and the Chief of Staff. He requested information from intelligence, from artillerymen, and I don't know who else. I don't think that I provided intelligence for any of the directives, either in a written form or verbal. It was the chief of sector, General Tolimir, who was in charge of that. He was the one who could request for the intel to be prepared for him, and I am not sure that I did it once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How did you learn that General Miletic participated in the drafting and in the preparation of this directive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never learnt that. I'm just telling you how things are done in principle. He was an operative. He was in charge of such matters. I'm sure that neither General Mladic now General Milovanovic would have done that. It would have been General Miletic. He was an operative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. They could have dictated things or provided input and their positions, and he was the one that did the technical part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this vital intelligence information is actually used to base the planned operations on, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. The first part of the directive talks about the enemy, the deployment of the enemy forces, the intentions and axis of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But in this particular case the chief of intelligence doesn't have any involvement in putting his stamp of approval or his analysis into this vital important information that was the basis, in part, for future military operations. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: What stamp are you referring to? There is no need for me to do that. The commander is the one who makes decisions on directives to be drafted. His assistants provide proposals for such directives. The chief of intelligence provides intel for the first part dealing with the enemy. The intelligence administration does that, and I may not have been there at the time. I suppose I wasn't. I didn't know that this was being done. My analyst could have provided the intel, but neither Miletic nor Tolimir were duty-bound to tell them why they needed the intel. They only told him that they needed intel about the enemy in Zepa, Srebrenica, or wherever else. Everything is updated on the map on a daily basis. The changes are input in the ops room where Miletic is seated. There is a big map with all the details and this is updated every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and we can see from this a lot of work went into it. It's a very long and complex document that -- you would agree with me that it took a matter of many days to put this document together so that it could be sent to the president, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The overall document, I don't know how long it is. I don't see all of it. I can see tasks, decisions. I suppose the Chief of Operations puts all the information together, words the entire document. That's what he did. You can see the commander's decision here. This is what I see here, and the task of the army. I'm sure that this is a long document. All directives were long documents, and they contained a lot of multidisciplinary areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, there's several reports that go out under your name, intel reports, in and around this time period, and we can see from them that they're very detailed, very -- they took a lot of work. Did you engage in reviewing that material that went out under your name, the daily reports of intel? Many of them we see are drafted by Karanovic and others. Did you review those daily intel reports before allowing them to go out under your name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I read them if I was there, and then I would sign the originals. However, if I wasn't there, I did not see them, I didn't sign them. I may have seen some of them subsequently. Some of them I didn't see at all. I would be absent for 10, 15 days at a time, and then they would give me the most important things on my return, because in my absence, a lot of things were received, not all of them equally important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would you meet with President Karadzic in Pale occasionally to discuss matters with him? This is -- after all, it's signed by him.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Never directly. All in all, three times during the war. But I was never on my own. Once there was a session of the Supreme Command, and in the absence of General Tolimir, I attended twice, and once on the eve of my travel abroad. There was a short meeting, a short discussion with him regarding my journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would he call you up and have discussions with you, talk to you about things?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. No. We submitted information to the office of the president. The office of the president received intel from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your extension number back in March of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I really don't know, believe me. I've lot of problems with retaining numbers, especially any numbers after 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we have what we believe is President Karadzic's appointment diary, and it shows that on March 4th, he called you, Colonel Salapura. Does that help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: When? The 4th of March? What year?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I apologise, what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if we could --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It is possible that that was on the eve of my travel abroad. And I also attended sessions of the Supreme Command, but when I attended on two occasions, no such matter was discussed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's take just -- if we can, a quick look at 65 ter 4840. And I am -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As we can see here, Colonel, this is the front page, and President Karadzic's secretaries have told us that if they put a plus by the mark, that means it happened and the president actually did it. And so if we go to page -- what's down here, page 7 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's currently on page 1 in English. If we could go to page 7. I'm sorry, I don't have the e-court page for that. You can -- well, sorry, it will ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I can see some things here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Twenty-seven, 27 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you can see that your name is mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The typed-up text, yes. I can see Professor Koljevic and Colonel Salapura. I can see it in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have the respective English page on the screen, please. The date, 4th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I haven't gotten there yet, Mr. President. I started with January. So this section is on there. It's down towards the bottom. But this is 18 January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then I notice another mention of your name on 24th January, and -- but let's go to the section that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, sorry. Mr. McCloskey, you used the entry of the 4th of March; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I said it, and then I asked them to go to the January entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm working my way there. I'm sorry about that confusion. So I will -- let's go to -- it's page 25 in the -- in the English. Well done. Down at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is 4 March, and Directive 7 came out 8 March, and this says: "Call Colonel Salapura - 226," and there's a plus by it meaning that that happened. Does this refresh your recollection? I think some of us would recall getting a call from the president of our respective countries.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment. The 4th. Just bear with me, please. The 4th of March. Budimir Kosutic. Yes. It says here "Call Colonel Salapura," correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I am not aware of having attended this at all. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. McCloskey tell us whether these were telephone conversations or whether these were invitations to meetings? We don't know what this is about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sure that Mr. McCloskey will try to get to that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, as far as I can tell, this is an appointment diary, and in the appointment diary of Dr. Karadzic he says "to call," and I'm telling you that we've been told by the secretaries that if there was a plus marked next to it that meant the call went through. All I'm asking you is whether or not this refreshes your recollection regarding speaking to the President of Republika Srpska four days here to --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. Well, I can see the plus. I can see "to call," which means that they did call me, I suppose, but I don't remember any such meeting, and especially when I see the names of these other people. Subotic, okay, the chief of office; Radiskovic, minister, I don't even know who that was; Djordje Ilic, I don't have a clue; Budo Kosutic, don't know. If there was a meeting, I don't know what it was about and I don't remember having attended it. And then there's this Italian name, Vincenzo Paglia. No, I don't remember having any such meeting. They may have called me. They may have an intention to call me, but I'm sure that I did not attend a meeting, especially not on the 4th [Realtime transcript read in error "14th"] of March 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey was not asking you about a meeting but a phone call by Mr. Karadzic. Do you recall a phone call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't remember such a phone call. I can't remember that President Karadzic called me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, it says March 14 on line 21. It should be March 4th, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I was just seeing if this jogged your memory in relation to Directive 7. I want to go back just briefly to Directive 7, page 12 --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- 14. Understand. All right. So I think we'll skip that and just try to keep going. Could we go to 65 ter 5810. And we see, sir, this is something from the Main Staff, dated 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. 27 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a list of documents for an operation --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's a list of documents for an operation called Sadejstvo. I'm sure that you can pronounce that better than I can. Submitted --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, Sadejstvo 95. And again I'm hearing of this code-name for the first time. I know nothing under that code-name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's submitted by General -- or Colonel Miletic. We know he is the Chief of Operations and Training of the Main Staff. And looking at number 7 here, it says that there's an intelligence support plan. Was your administration involved in writing up an intelligence support plan for this operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: On the left list of documents, Sadejstvo operation plan, intelligence support. No. What it says here, it says order for intelligence support, intelligence support plan. Yes. Yes. The administration probably did write that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, do you recall it?
