utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. And I affirm that I did not attend, and I was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go to 65 ter 32.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: With full responsibility, with all certainty, because I don't remember that name at all, Sadejstvo 95. I don't remember any involvement by me personally. By the administration, possibly. I'm not ruling that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at this we see it's the first page of a plan for intelligence support of the Main Staff for Operation Sadejstvo 95. Now, I think you'll agree with me that --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute. No, no. Sorry. This has nothing to do with it. This has to do with the Srecko Polje operation in Tuzla. That operation was planned and never executed. It was an order from the commander to make a plan for an operation at the level the Main Staff involving the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska and a specific corps of it, and I believe half of it was never carried out. This was never carried out, and there were indeed many operations that were planned and prepared but never carried out, and this has nothing to do whatsoever with Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now you remember this operation and know about -- and you know about it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it was called the Sadejstvo or not, I know that such an operation existed, was prepared. And we were aware in advance that we were not going to be able to carry it out, that we did not have enough forces. However, it was planned at the orders of the commander and never done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next page. And we see about the zones of responsibility that this is involved in, 1st Krajina Corps, East Bosnia Corps. Is this the operation you're thinking of?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. This is what was planned. Gracanica, Dubrava, Srecko Polje. Yes, that's it, but that operation was never carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you know about these documents that planned for it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know about this. I know about the operation. I know it was planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page. And here we -- we see your name with a "za" in front of it, a "for the chief of intelligence administration." Can you see your name written down there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Somebody signed for me, somebody who was standing in for me at the time. Let me look at the signature. It's Karanovic -- no, it's Radoslav Jankovic who signed it. I didn't. That means I wasn't there at the time when this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But since it went out in your name, it would have been something that you would have made yourself familiar with, like you just testified?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, if that was the operation that I was talking about. If it is. But I'm telling you I wasn't doing this. I know this was planned, but I did not work on these elements. I just wasn't there. I was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: How can I remember after 15 years or 19? How can I remember where exactly I was at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P1199.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 65 ter 5810 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. We need to -- the one I was referring to was the plan that had his name on it, and that is 65 ter 00032. I'm sorry, I wasn't very clear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you didn't tender the -- that one I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I should -- I should offer that into evidence as well. That is 65 ter 05810, and that was the list of the intel documents. I should have. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And to avoid complications, we have received that as P2196. And in addition you want which one into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the diary or the agenda of Mr. Karadzic? I don't think that we need the whole one, but you have used one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. The page from March 4th would be 0 -- the whole thing is 04840. It may be used again. Ms. Stewart suggests I just MFI it, and I think that would be a good idea, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be P2198, marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, now we see on the screen from the Main Staff again, 31 March 1995. It's entitled under "National Defence State Secret Sadejstvo 95," and it's called a "Directive for Further Operations, Operation No. 7/1." I won't go through all the pages, but in the English it's several pages. Eight pages, signed at the end by General Mladic, again drafted by Miletic. This would have taken a long time, I'm sure, to get together, and this is -- this is the operation you now remember; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the operation that was planned, that the Main Staff was supposed to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you should have reviewed this plan. In fact, you should have taken part in it. Your unit -- your administration should have taken part in this, and you should have reviewed --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I was not involved in the preparation of these documents. I was involved when the commander decided this, that an operation would be planned to be carried out by the Main Staff and the corps at its own level. I remember that conversation clearly, and I said that it was perpetuum mobile. I used those words. I said the Main Staff can write anything they like, but we don't have enough forces to actually carry this out. And that's what I know. I know it was never carried out, and I was not involved in this, but I know it was planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2 of this document in English, and it should be number 2 in -- in the B/C/S. Paragraph 2 called "The task of the VRS." And we can see the first line here, blow that up, under "Task of the VRS," and it says: "On the basis of Directive 7," and then it goes on to lists the tasks in detail. Directive 7 is mentioned in this a few times. It's actually itself called Directive 7/1. So anyone involved in this document and reading this document would certainly have to have reviewed Directive 7, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Who was involved in this preparation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Simple question, Colonel. We can see that the reference is on the basis of Directive 7. So can't we conclude that if someone is involved in drafting this information they would have had to review Directive 7 since this is based on Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, they would have been involved, yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you were involved and you knew about this Sadejstvo operation, you would have needed to know about Directive 7 as well.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Directive 7 was issued for the Main Staff, for the command and control of one whole operation, and now what this is about, Sarajevo, Trnovo, Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, Colonel, did you know about this operation Sadejstvo? I thought you said you did. The one that was never done, in your view.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I knew, but I don't know what this is. I know that that operation was planned at the level of the Main Staff, Srecko Polje. That's what I remember, that it should be carried out using certain forces, et cetera, et cetera, and I know that never happened. Now, perhaps this is a component of that operation, a certain segment. I don't know the details. I don't know what was envisaged, because I wasn't directly involved in the preparation of these documents, I was just there when the idea was conceived by the commander. I was there when -- when he was thinking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to another topic. We'll work our way towards the 12th, as you've mentioned briefly, but you were still at Crna Rijeka until about somewhere around July 20th or thereafter, 20 to 25th, as you've said -- excuse me, June 20th or 25th. And so I'd like to ask you: Were you aware of the operation, the military operation, to take down OP Echo at Zeleni Jadar that occurred on about June 3rd, 1995, and was the prelude to the upcoming attack on the Srebrenica enclave by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. No, I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 5886.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, this is one report, and you can see that it's a Regular Combat Report from the Drina Corps command on 3 June, to the Main Staff and to the Chief of Staff personally. And it begins by: "After the successful operation and the forceful expulsion of UNPROFOR from the Zeleni Jadar post, the enemy was observed," systematically, "building up large forces ..." et cetera. Certainly you would have heard about this either on June 3rd when it happened or before or shortly thereafter as part of intelligence information leading up to the decision to the attack the Srebrenica enclave. Is that fair or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I never heard of this for sure. Absolutely. This is an operation involving the forces of our corps. You see who's sending it, and as for me, I did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Let me tell you straight away. If I had that information, I would have reacted, because I was strongly against any kind of action against the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, were you familiar with any of the planning that went into the plan to attack the Srebrenica enclave in June and July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: What do you mean, plans or planning? I know only about one operation carried out by the 10th Sabotage Detachment in Srebrenica, passing through a tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we know about that. That was on or about the 20 --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That's all I know. As for these other activities of the Drina Corps, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you know about the attack through the tunnel that we've heard about from Mr. Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And I've followed that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you never heard anything about the -- the attack on UNPROFOR OP Echo, and you never heard anything about the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, which occurred on the 6th -- on or about the 6th of July? Just a -- two weeks after the tunnel attack?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I left after that operation through the tunnel. It was just a display of force with no consequences. It was a warning to the forces in the Srebrenica enclave that they should not mount any sabotage or other actions against Serbs, because there had been such operations against the Main Staff and our forces. There had been incursions into our territory, killing soldiers and civilians. That was the purpose of that operation, and I can explain that, if you want me, in greater detail, but I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, even though you were, as you told us yourself, receiving information from Banja Luka, from your subordinates. I just want to be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I received certain information, what they considered to be relevant for me in Banja Luka, but believe me, those were only intelligence reports that I received - but there is not a single report, or perhaps you can find it because you have all of them - where this is written, because the commander had strictly prohibited this should be written about. That's an explanation I heard later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, what makes you think we have all the reports? We have a fraction of the reports. What makes you think the Prosecution has all the reports?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, I think you certainly have 1.000 more than I have, because there were many seizure and search operations. But if you allow me to say this: Just before I left for Banja Luka, precisely at the moment when I asked for written approval and finally went to Banja Luka with General Tolimir - let him recall this if he can - he asked me, "What do you think about the enclaves?" I said, "Which ones?" He said, "Zepa and Srebrenica." I said, "In my view, we should not touch them at all, by no means. That would be very counter-productive and would cause a very negative reaction." And his answer was, "I think these are ripe apples, and I share your opinion." I asked ask him what, how, with what purpose. That was the end of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He used the term "ripe apples"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Actually, he said, "pears."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did General Tolimir say they were "ripe pears"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. But why? He probably meant that those were weak, insufficient forces under the protection of the United Nations, and any action against them would only cause an outcry. But pressure needed to be exerted on the UN to really demilitarise the area and not to allow any provocations coming from the protected area. And you also have reports, probably, from the 28th Division addressed to Tuzla. They are exceptional. And you will see in their own reports how many casualties we suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel. We agree with that basic premise, and we always have, and we have prosecuted some people, perhaps not enough, but let me ask you, you mentioned the documents, did you ever make an effort to find some documents before you came to testify the first time, or your own notes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. Well, yes, I did make an effort, but I couldn't. I did not have access. When I was coming to testify here, I was already a retired officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you informed that they were burned or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that quite a lot of the materials were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- and who -- who or -- who told you that or what position were they, if you're sensitive about the name? What position of the person told you that the materials from the past that you were interested in had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was asking for some of my notebooks and documents that were mine, and then I was told that they can't be found because they had been destroyed or burned. Well, you know, maybe I would have done the same if I were there, because there were certain names mentioned there, contacts, I mean, that shouldn't have been. You know, material of operative nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, who told you that materials, intelligence materials, had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, I would have to remember the face of the person who was in the intelligence administration after me. Samardzic. He was the chief, and now I don't know who was in charge of the archives, what the name of that person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it was the --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: But I do know that some of the official documents and reports were handed over to a team of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We do have some things, as you're finding out. Now, let me go back to the tunnel attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move to -- back to that, I have a follow-up question. Sir, you said on page 53, lines 14 and 15: "The commander had strictly prohibited this should be written about." Who told you that the commander - I think you're referring to Mr. Mladic - had strictly prohibited to write anything down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say write anything down. That nothing should be written down during the course of the operation. I assume he wanted to make sure that it remained secret during the course of the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I read it out to you again. I quote: "But there is not a single report, or perhaps you can find it because you have all of them, where there is written, because the commander had strictly prohibited this should be written about." This is what I can find in the record. Could you explain that further, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just told you about this. This concerned intelligence information and reports that we were sending at the time when the Srebrenica operation was in progress. There was nothing, because as I was told, it had been prohibited by the commander, namely none of the reports were supposed to be sent during the progress of the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you. Please respond to me. I would like to know who told you this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was Mamlic, at the command post when I went there. I think it was him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And when you say "prohibited by the commander," you are referring to General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably. He was the commander. If the commander prohibited it, that means it was him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, I was asking you if he prohibited that anything should be written down. You didn't answer that question. You were telling me none of the reports were supposed to be sent during the progress of the operation. To write something down or to send a report, these are different things. I want to know what the command -- why and what the commander meant when he -- sorry. Please wait. I want to know what do you mean by nothing should be written down. These are your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the commander meant. What I'm talking about are intelligence reports that are normally drafted. Nothing was drafted about the course of the operation in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where and when did the person with the name Mamlic tell you about that? What exactly did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told by, at the time when I was at the command post, so on the 13th or the 14th - I'm not certain about the date - but I was told then that they were not receiving information about the course of Srebrenica operation so that they cannot forward those to their units. So they were not receiving reports from the subordinated units, from units subordinated to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you. I think it was Mamlic. He was the only person I'm certain that was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An officer. He was an officer in charge of electronic reconnaissance in the intelligence administration of the Main Staff, and at the time he was the only person present in the administration. I was away. Another man was in Belgrade. One man was in SFOR base. He was the only person present at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you mentioned to the President that you were at the command post, was that -- do you mean the Main Staff command post at Crna Rijeka on or about the 13th or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: At Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's talk a bit about this tunnel operation of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. And what involvement, if any, did you have in that attack or the plan or the use of the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In what capacity --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: In proposing. The command of the Drina Corps asked the commander for that kind of engagement, and then the commander told me to review the situation and to see whether it was feasible to carry it out. I went, and I cannot give you any exact dates. I went to the command of the Drina Corps. There was a detachment commander, Pelemis, there was Popovic, who was chief of security, and there was Golic, Pavle Golic as well, and they explained how they intended to carry out the operation, if the operation would be carried out. I heard them out. I provided them with some elements that should be carried out and finalised in more detail in order to make sure that there would be no casualties among UNPROFOR troops or the civilian population and yet to succeed in warning the opposing side because that was our intention. And on the next occasion the detachment commander provided me with full elaboration of the plan, and I told the commander later on that it's feasible that it can be carried out with any risk -- without any risk, and the mission was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who issued the order to carry it out to the -- to the -- to the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The commander. The commander of the Main Staff. He approved the mission based on a request of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we understand, as you've testified briefly, that the 10th Sabotage Detachment could be used for intel purposes and that you proposed its various uses for things, and we discussed about monitoring and that kind of thing, so we -- I understand that fits basically with what you've just said, and I -- can you tell us, you've mentioned Pavle Golic. What's his position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He was a security officer in the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Pavle Golic security or intel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Intelligence. Intelligence. Popovic was security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So I understand that this Sabotage Detachment can be used as an intel asset for reconnaissance, and so I see your involvement. I understand your involvement. I understand Pavle Golic's involvement, but why would a security officer of the Drina Corps, Vujadin Popovic, be involved?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain how it is that a security officer would be involved in what is -- in this sort of operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It was upon their request, the request of the command of the Drina Corps, because this was an operation in their area of operations. They were the ones most familiar with the terrain. I didn't know the terrain there. They came up with the proposal. They know the situation better than anyone else, all the features.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if Popovic had a particular need for the 10th Sabotage Detachment and the Drina Corps had that, they would go through you in order to use it, like they did in this tunnel attack? By the rules and regulations, I mean.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: According to rules and regulations and also in accordance with order establishing this detachment, that the detachment can be used anywhere in the zone of operations of the VRS. It -- they can be used on the basis of our proposal, namely the intelligence administration, or on the basis of requests coming in from various corps. In this particular occasion it was upon a request of the command of the Drina Corps. I think it was a request made by the Chief of Staff, Krstic, and he asked that of the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you inform General Tolimir of this proposal -- of this request and proposal?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I believe so. If he was present. Although, I think Tolimir may have been absent. No, no, I did. I think I did. Or he may have been absent and joined only later, because I know that the commander initially gave that personally to me. So my guess would be that Tolimir was not initially there but was made aware later that this was carried out. It is possible that he was absent at the start of the operation, but I really cannot remember all the details concerning this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't want you to guess. If General Tolimir was there, would he have had to know about the potential use of this important asset?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He would, and I would have informed him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he would have had his say in whether or not it was appropriate to use the 10th Sabotage for this sort of a -- sort of a thing, I take it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: But once the commander has given an order or an instruction to review this -- let me explain how it went. The command of the Drina Corps, the command of the Main Staff. The commander told me personally, because Tolimir most probably was absent. So the commander asked me to look into the feasibility of their request. I went to the Drina Corps command. There was also the commander of the detachment there, the commander of security and intelligence organs. I reviewed the situation. They presented -- they briefed me on the situation, rather. They told me about how and when it was supposed to be done. I asked them to come back to me with additional information, and after two or three days, and I even asked for everything to be recorded --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've explained all that, Colonel, and my only point is if General Tolimir was there, he would have had his say in whether this important asset was used; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, most probably then the chain would go the other way. The request would go to General Mladic, who would then pass it on to Tolimir, who would then pass it on to me. Since in this case General Mladic passed it directly to me, that means to me that General Tolimir was absent, but he was made aware about this mission and that the detachment carried it out. Well, I cannot tell you whether that was still during the preparation stage or after the mission was accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who had more authority over the 10th Sabotage Detachment, you as the chief of the intel branch, or General Tolimir as the boss of the intel and security sector?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Myself, I would have more authority. They knew me better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're telling me in a military it -- authority depends on how well you know someone? Doesn't rank and position play a role in the use of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, sir? We're not idiots.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: You know, I was more often in contact with the commander. I was more in charge of professional monitoring. General Tolimir, of course, had less, but he was higher ranking, and his position was higher, but, yes, I was the one who was monitoring that more than anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you would be reporting to General Tolimir about what you were monitoring and your use of the 10th Sabotage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I was reporting, yes, about all the operations where I, first of all, proposed and then monitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember in the Blagojevic case you -- I think you told me that you were angry at General Tolimir for the use of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, I agree, but not for this mission. Let's not mix things up. It was because it was used not for its usual task. It was used in Srebrenica for combat activities, attack activities. That was the information I'd received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- so why were you angry at -- at Tolimir for the 10th being used in a combat activity? And we'll get into that in a little more detail, but why were you angry at him for that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly sit closer to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, it was not for the first time, and it wasn't that I was only angry at him. In the order concerning the establishment of this detachment, the commander specifically said that this detachment can be used exclusively for sabotage and similar actions, whereas this was not that kind of a mission. Any unit could have carried out that mission. The troops we're talking about here were not trained for that kind of operations. Those operations are something for the infantry. These people were trained for more complex missions behind the enemy lines, reconnaissance duties that are very risky, and not anyone can carry them out, that's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that, and I think everyone does. And you've said you weren't in the area and didn't know anything about the attack on Srebrenica, so General Tolimir, in your view, must have been the one that approved the use of the 10th Sabotage for the attack on Srebrenica? I'm talking about July now, not the tunnel in June.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Please, let us not mix things up, because if we are imprecise, nothing good's going to come out of that. Tolimir could not have approved for detachments to be used for missions that are not strictly part of their normal type of assignment. Only the commander could have done that. And I was angry at Tolimir because he did not put in an extra effort and try and convince the commander not to use them for that. That period, one segment was in the area of Modrica in the zone of the 1st Krajina Corps, and this other group was supposed to go to Herzegovina to the zone of the Hercegovina Corps in order to do reconnaissance in the area of Dubrovnik. Instead, they were sent to carry out infantry tasks, and that was why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. We must have our second break now, and we will resume at quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I need to offer that last document about the Zeleni Jadar operation - it was 65 ter 05886 - into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel, before we get back into the chronology, I was going in one direction when we were talking about a while back about your knowledge of General Tolimir. You were in the academy with him. You obviously spent the war working closely with him. Could you just tell us, describe for us your friendship or your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, are you friends after all those years together in the war? Do you consider him a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, you know what? I consider him a friend, if I may say so, but we're both soldiers, and our relationship was based on that, on the relationship of a superior and a subordinate. Throughout my military career, I always avoided establishing friendly relationships with my subordinates. I always wanted to keep them at an official distance, and that same applied to commanders, chiefs, everybody. That was my principle, something that I adhered to until I retired. We were in good terms. I respected him, and I consider him -- I don't know. Do you want me to hear -- do you want me to share with you my opinion of him? I don't know what you want from me. But when it comes to being close friends, socialising, families visiting each other, no, that was not the case. We were together at the command post. He never visited me in my apartment, and vice versa, I never visited him. I met his wife, but he didn't meet mine. He doesn't know anybody, any members of my family. I never contacted him in my private capacity or the other way round. Our friendship was never put to a test. We were just co-workers, and I respected him greatly as a soldier and as a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's what I was asking about. Now, unfortunately, let's get back to the summer of 1995 and this -- a little more on this tunnel operation. You've said it was -- something about -- to get their attention or -- what was the purpose of this attack again? I've forgotten precisely what you said, but can you tell us what was the purpose of this operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The purpose of this operation was warning. The Muslim side was sent a signal to stop provocations from the protected area. To stop with incursions into our territory, to stop inflicting casualties among the civilians and soldiers. They were in the protected zone. And the second thing was to put pressure on UNPROFOR, to disarm the demilitarized zone or to prevent incursions being launched from the protected area. We wanted incursions to be stopped against the VRS. We wanted to flex muscle and show them that we were capable of launching similar operations. And I believe that the operation was done correctly. It was a demonstration of force rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what kind of force? What were they supposed to do, these members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I said the nature of the operation was to show them that we were able to enter the city and launch an operation there. The target was the police station where the command of the brigade was. However, we didn't carry that out completely because of poor visibility. It was foggy. It was 4.00 in the morning, I think. As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what kind of weapons were designed to be used inside this city? We all know the centre of the police station is right there in the centre of the city. You went by it. What kind of weapons would you be using against the police station?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Infantry weapons. The aim was not to destroy the police station. There were very few men there at the time. It was not our intention to inflict big, heavy losses on them, so we used normal weapons, infantry weapons, and hand-held rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So hand-held rocket launchers in the -- were going to be used against the police station in the middle of this populated city?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on line 67, the witness's answer was not properly recorded, because the witness said more than was recorded. I believe that he mentioned the calibre of the weaponry and some other things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you mean by that. It's a hand-held rocket launcher which is used against facilities. It's a 70-millimetre rocket launcher for one-time use. These are not real rocket. This is something that a soldier carries on his shoulder, and a bullet can pierce the wall and enter a room. It can go through glass. It's a -- they use rounds in urban areas. They are intended to be used against facilities, buildings in an urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at a document, 65 ter 7293.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this has a star next to it. This is not one that we got a 65 ter number for, but I've spoken briefly with Mr. Gajic, and I have not heard any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, could we go to the second page of the B/C/S just so you could see whose name this is under first. Now, the English translation says "Chief Colonel Petar Salapura."

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I signed this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So then let's give you a chance to look at it from the beginning then. Just tell us when you're through so we can go to the next page. And we can see from the English that this is from the Main Staff, sector for intel and security. It's signed by you, as you've just said, dated 21 June 1995. Very urgent, to the command of the Drina Corps intelligence department, and for the commander of the 10th DOd. Can you tell us what the 10th DOd is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see that it's order for engagement of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. And we can see that -- I won't read it all out, but it talks about 21 June, started intensive preparation --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- to carry out sabotage activities at the ordered time and selected features. It says: "Develop a detailed plan by 1000 hours on the 22nd of June, and brief me about the decision at 1200 hours on 22 June. The commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment and the chief of intelligence at the department of the Drina Corps are responsible for gathering data, planning the execution of the task." It talks about taking reconnaissance. Number 3 says: "The chief of the intelligence department of the Drina Corps shall co-ordinate the work with the units in contact and be in command of the complete operation." So who was in command of this ground operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The commander of the operation was the commander of the detachment, Pelemis. And the chief of the intelligence department co-ordinated everything. You can see what had to be secured, what intelligence had to be provided in order for the operation to take place. So you can see what happened before the operation and during the operation, the overall co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, in the -- and perhaps it's a translation issue, but in the English, it reads: "The chief of the intelligence department of the Drina Corps shall co-ordinate the work with the units in contact and be in command of the complete operation." In English this says that the chief of intel is in command of the operation. Is that not right in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Please, the original, but now we come to a situation where you have to give me 10 to 15 minutes. I have to give you all the details. This is a matter of profession. Where it says here the -- the commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment and chief of the Drina Corps intelligence department will be responsible for collection -- collecting intelligence, planning and carrying out the task. These are several different activities that are enumerated here. After detailed reconnaissance --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just asking about number 3. And you know your language better than I do. In English it says that the commander of this operation is the Drina Corps chief of intel. So based on what number 3 says, who's the commander of this operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Please. Please. If you will allow me. We're talking about co-ordination, a co-ordinated activity. I suppose that can be translated into English. Co-ordination with units in contact shall be carried out by the chief of the intelligence department of the Drina Corps, and he will control the entire activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We just heard --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: And now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who is controlling the entire activity of this operation from the ground?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The intelligence organ of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The intelligence organ of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And who was that at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I believe that that was either Kosoric or Golic. I don't know which of the two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if it was Major Golic and Lieutenant-Colonel Svetozar Kosoric, does that help reflect your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Kosoric, yes. Well, I can't remember. I know that Kosoric was sick and he was very often on sick leaves. I don't know whether he was on a sick leave at the time. I know that he was present when I was handing out tasks, but Golic was also there because he used to stand in for Golic. So I don't know which one of the two was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is this an order you issued?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, pursuant to our commander's order, the commander of the Main Staff. I was the one who gave him a proposal. He approved it. He wrote it and gave it to me to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you can issue an order that's consistent with an order of the commander.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, based on the commander's orders. Like here. I don't know how this is entitled. This is entitled, "An order for the use of a unit based on the commander's order," and there's co-ordination between the detachment and the Drina Corps, i.e., the latter's intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you can issue an order like this that is consistent with the commander's order, General Tolimir would also be able to issue an order that is consistent with a commander's order. Generally, I'm speaking. If you can do it, General Tolimir can do it. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He could have, but most probably he wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: And he could have passed it on to somebody else. It could have been regulated by the intelligence administration. For example, I could have been the one to regulate this. The commander -- the commander of the detachment issued his order in turn, and he was also the one who issued an order, and that order would also concern the use of his detachment based on the previous orders that he had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: How is it that you think General Tolimir wasn't there? You yourself weren't very clear about any of these dates. Why are you now telling us that you don't think General Tolimir was there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, he may have been or not. He could have conveyed the order to me orally, or it could have been given to me by the commander directly. I don't know what happened. No, I know. In this particular case it was given to me directly by the commander because Tolimir wasn't there. If Tolimir had been there, I would have received the order through Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, I am telling you what the procedure was. I remember that it was the commander personally who had given me the task to regulate the whole matter and to co-ordinate with the Drina Corps, because this was done at a request of the command of the Drina Corps, and it was done in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go to the paragraph 4. It says --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: And you can see what we insisted on. Look at bullet point 6. Look at what needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're going to get there, I promise, but let's --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Very well. It doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, number 4 says: "Inform the Drina Corps Chief of Staff about the task." Remind us who that was at the time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Perhaps it was Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Drina Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. I apologise. The Chief of Staff was Krstic at the time, and Zivanovic was commander. Now I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why -- what was Krstic's special significance here that he is the one that's getting informed as opposed to his commander? If you know.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Because the intelligence organs were involved here, and he was subordinated to the Chief of Staff of the corps, and the Chief of Staff was supposed to inform the commander and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: He was the -- he was Golic's immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. As well as -- was he Popovic's superior as well as Chief of Staff and deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. No. The commander was Popovic's superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. He was his commander, but was General Krstic a superior of Popovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No. Not at that moment. Zivanovic was Popovic's superior as the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to paragraph 5. It says: "Engage the complete detachment for the execution of this task. Complete the task (activity) within 10 to 15 minutes." So that's a pretty brief task. What is that task that's supposed to only take 10 to 15 minutes? I mean, we can't have coffee around here in 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, the task did not have a goal to destroy, demolish, or occupy Srebrenica. The mission was to flex muscle and to warn the other side without any casualties on any of the sides. It was just a demonstration of power, after which the unit withdrew very quickly. When I learned that the rain was -- that the area was foggy, I curtailed the duration of the mission down to maybe five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, and we'll all notice and we'll get to the second page and the Geneva Conventions in a minute, but we'll all notice there is no detail in here. We don't know where this is. We don't even know this has anything to do with Srebrenica. How do you know it has anything to do with Srebrenica? Does it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I know that the mission was accomplished at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, how do we know that document is related to the tunnel -- what we call the tunnel operation? There's no mention of a tunnel. There's no mention of a location.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: That was that. That was that. No. It would be the commander who would have elaborated all that. The -- the detachment commander. These are just basic outlines, things that needed to be done, things that needed to be carried out. A co-ordination needed to be carried out, and the detachment commander had to elaborate the whole thing and provide all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I understand that, but it's very clear from this document that there are no specifics in it. Was that done deliberately for security purposes, in case this got in the hands of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, no, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just happenstance there's not one indication of what -- where this is? There's no Srebrenica. There's no tunnel. There's no weapons. There's nothing except times.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: There was no need to mention any of that. This is a document for preparations. It was a document for the commander to elaborate. There had been a prior conversation with them, and they knew what the operation was about. The commander approved the operation, and it was up to them to embark on an elaboration, and the commander of the detachment had to draft his own order where he would elaborate the time, the place, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page in English so we can see everything, and that would be -- it's paragraph -- you want to get paragraph 5 and 6 in the B/C/S. I can't, unfortunately, see the thing on my screen in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so we see here that: "The exact time shall be decided by the detachment commander with the consent of the Drina Corps chief of intelligence. "Extraction of the detachment from the activity zone, carry out a long infiltration route under smoke protection." And then number 6: "During the execution of the task adhere strictly to the following: The UNPROFOR staff are not to be put in danger, avoid casualties among women and children, make sure you capture live sources." So was part of this operation to capture people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "In case of wounding or death of any detachment member, the same has to be extracted at any cost and no soldier can fall into enemy hands." I think we understand that. "Before departure on a task, seize all the identification documents from all soldiers." I think we understand that. "Secure the complete secrecy of the operation in terms of place and time." We understand that. "Use the communication means upon the given signal for the start of the activities, applying only TKT." What's TKT?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Secret commanding of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. "Develop several possible methods and an alternative axis of retreat. In case of need, secure the artillery support of the units in contact and plan the fire according to the agreed signal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I notice that you are reading from a translation. It seems not to be the same translation as we have on the screen, because there are quite a lot of differences. It is the same content, of course, but this is another translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can see that you're absolutely correct, Mr. President, and we will try to make sure that we get you the best translation. That happens sometimes, and I don't know if I am -- which one I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to put it on the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, and -- I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you hear anything that's not quite right about the translation, you'll let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, but we have to make sure that the right translation is -- will be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll look into that, Mr. President, and see if one is better than the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That remains an open question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now go to P961.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, what I'm going to show now is a -- it's a report from the Dutch Battalion of Srebrenica to their sector headquarters north-east is what they call it. It's dated the 24th of June, 1995. And under paragraph 2 on the first page, it says: "Srebrenica." And then we need to go to the next page in the English. And I want to -- there's a part titled "Reconstruction of the events." So I think we need to go to the next page in the B/C/S. Yes. And I want to start, yeah, with that part, because it's a bit of a summary, and it says: "A group of unknown strength set up fire positions on two locations (where the longitudes were found). They fired their projectile simultaneously into Srebrenica. One man was injured when the projectile struck his house. After the attack, personnel of the firing teams retreated to the mine entrance under cover of mortar fire. Nineteen grenades were fired from the vicinity of the mine entrance. It is not sure whether another mortar from outside the enclave delivered the supporting fire. Two people fled from their house in the Vitlovac near the mine entrance in the direction of Srebrenica. They probably surprised some of the people of the raid group who were waiting near the mine entrance. They were shot with an M," something that I can't tell, "killing the woman and injuring the man. The raid group probably retreated through the mine. Comment: It is most likely but not confirmed they were BSA," meaning Bosnian Serb Army. "The BiH did not notice any action, nor did DutchBat." So this description, that has to be the event that we're talking about from the perspective of DutchBat; correct? However -- whatever report that they received.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So basically your unit went in with about 19 shoulder-fired missiles, fired them into the town, hitting a house, and on your way out killed two civilians. Is that the report you got afterward?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: I did not receive any information about the casualties. Until now we did not have exact information about that. What I did learn was that a woman, I think, was killed and a child was wounded. That's the information I got. Where, how, and under what circumstances and from whose fire, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that killing of the woman is consistent with this report. So in your view, did going into that tunnel and firing off --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Going into that tunnel, coming out into Srebrenica town and firing your 19 missiles into this crowded town, did that get the mission accomplished? Did that do what you were trying to do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, it was not fired into a crowd, and these projectiles were not fired to hit someone, because they did not hit anything. I told you, it was a show of force. It was foggy, and there was no visibility. That's how it ended up this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you see anything wrong with firing 19 --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: What was fired -- no, I can't see, and it says 19 missiles. I don't know if it's 19 or how many. It wasn't in the report I got. And it's certainly not a mortar. I believe those were not mortar shells. I think those were all hand-held launchers, and that was during extraction that they fired to protect themselves while entering the tunnel, in case anybody was pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in your view did it -- was it good military sense to go in and point these hand-held rockets and shoot it into this town in the fog, at people's houses? We see a house gets hit. Was that -- was that the purpose of this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, that was not the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see from your order that --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: But it was foggy, and one was fired. One did go out. You can call it collateral damage. It happened. It's war. Regardless of how many orders you give to take care of civilians and avoid civilian casualties, these things happen. Even on a football pitch, people play football and somebody gets hurt. It's a combat mission, but there was no targeting of civilians, that's for sure. A round went astray. And it could have been, by the way, a bullet, not a shell, not a rocket. I can't see from this where this woman was exactly, where she happened to be, or these two people. This is not quite clear to me. Some two people fled, then fire was opened, and the woman got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So going into a UN protected enclave and firing 19 shoulder-fired rockets, which in the direction is not -- you don't see any military issue with that at all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Well, I've told you what the objective was, what the purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, this --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: The objective of this operation was to avoid what later eventually happened. The purpose was to put an end to provocations from Srebrenica so that we would not be forced to take any action against Srebrenica. That was our purpose and our desire. That the SFOR should warn them -- or, rather, UNPROFOR, because -- because UNPROFOR was informed by our side of all our losses and all our casualties, and they were unable to prevent them, these attacks coming from Srebrenica, because it was never demilitarised. Even if they were not demilitarised, the protection they enjoyed from UN forces should not have been abused in that way, but I won't go into explaining that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we've heard evidence here that in Directive 7 that apparently you've never heard of, that Karadzic ordered that life be made impossible for the inhabitants of Srebrenica. The security and intel officer of the Bratunac Brigade has testified that there was a campaign to snipe civilians and to make their life miserable, and wasn't it -- wasn't this particular operation designed to help terrorise the inhabitants? Wasn't that why you go shoot 19 rockets into the downtown area of Srebrenica on June 24th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. This operation had a completely different objective. Its objective was to avoid precisely what you're talking about. This operation had absolutely nothing to do with that. As for the projectiles that were fired into the air, it has nothing to do with this. This was just a show of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel -- Colonel --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Second, all these are assumptions, and I swear on my life that there was never such an idea. It never crossed anybody's mind, whatever you are trying to infer. I was a combatant throughout that war. I viewed all the events in Srebrenica as an outsider, through the eyes of the international community. That was our job, and that's precisely what I was trying to avoid. I was trying to have the situation in Srebrenica calm down, to stop the provocations against our units and against civilians on our side and so on. This has nothing to do with that. This has nothing to do with Karadzic's directive, and I affirm with full responsibility, I swear on my life, that I never knew it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that needs to be the last word for the night, and I won't have any more questions for tonight, but I will for tomorrow. And, Mr. President, we've been going longer than I thought. I hope not to take -- I'll have to look at my material, but I would say if I could ask for another hour, that would be safer. But I may be being too hard on myself as well, but I'm just feeling it at this point that these answers and the length and things are a bit longer than I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will see how it turns out tomorrow. Thank you very much. Sir, we have to adjourn for the day. We will continue tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15 in this courtroom, Courtroom I. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of May, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
